Abul Quasem Bhuiyan with B.M. Nowab Zakaria, Advocates ------ For the appellants 
A.F.M. Shahid, Asstt. Attorney General ------ For respondent 3
parties:
Nannu Miah & Others
Vs.
Bangladesh through the Deputy Commissioner & Others
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J: — This appeal by the plaintiffs is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26-4-78 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 100 of 1977 dismissing the same and affirming those of the learned Munsif, 2nd court, Brahmanbaria passed in Title suit No. 167 of 1973. Plaintiffs brought the aforesaid suit for a declaration that Memo No. 1768/E.P dated 6-8-68 of defendant no. 2 declaring the plaint scheduled property as enemy property was illegal, void etc. and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with the plaintiffs' peaceful possession in the suit property and giving effect to Memo No. 635(3) dated 29-8-73. Plaintiffs' case is that 09 decimals of land as described in the schedule to the plaint originally belonged to one Nirenjan Roy Barman who while being in possession of the same made a will dated 6-10-63 in respect of the said land in favour of his wife Banalata Roy Barman for her future maintenance. Niranjan Roy Barman died on 17-1-67 at his own residence at Bidyakot in the District of Comilla. In view of the will executed by him, his sons did not and could not acquire any right in the suit property. Banalata Roy Barman applied to the District Judge for probate of the said will and, accordingly, the District Judge granted probate to Banalata Roy Barman on 3-4-72 in Probate case no. 270 of 1969. Thus Banalata became the rightful owner of the suit property and she sold the same to the plaintiffs by different registered sale deeds dated 27-6-72. The plffs. have been in possession of the suit land since their purchase. They received a notice on 12-5-73 from the defend-ant No.1 asking them to show cause against eviction from the suit property on the allegation that they were in unauthorised and illegal possession of the same. The plaintiffs showed cause as directed but the defendant no.1 illegally asked the plaintiffs to surrender possession of the suit property by 30-8-73. On pain of being forcibly evicted there from by police force whereupon the plaintiffs immediately instituted the present suit i.e. on 30-8-73 and prayed for an order of injunction restraining the defendants as aforesaid. 

 3. Defendants no.1, Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria, contested the suit by filing a written statement. Besides denying the allegations of the plaintiffs, various pleas were raised as to the non-maintained is that the owner of the disputed property Niranjan Roy Barman died in the then East Pakistan leaving behind three sons as his heirs who have been permanently living in India and, as such, the suit property was declared as enemy property by the Assistant Custodian of Enemy property (L & B), Comilla by his Memo. No. 1768/E.P. dated 6-8-68. It is claimed that the plaintiffs by their purchase from Banalata Roy in 1972 did not acquire any interest in the suit property as the same already vested in the Government as enemy property. The defendant asserted that the unauthorised occupants were asked to surrender possession and upon receipt of such notice Abu Sayed Bhuiyan and others surrendered their possession to the Tahsilder on 29-8-73. Upon the pleadings of the parties, issues, as to the maintainability of the suit, puffs' title and limitation were raised. The learned Munsif upon a consideration of the evidence on record found that the plaintiffs has acquired no title to the suit land by their purchase from Banalata Roy Barman and the suit was also barred by limitation. Accordingly, the suit was dismissed and on appeal by the plffs. the decree was affirmed by the learned subordinate Judge Hence this appeal. 

 4. The Subordinate Judge merely endorsed the findings of the trial court without properly assessing the evidence himself. He, however, made certain findings on the basis of the arguments advanced by the Government pleader on behalf of the respondent. It is apparent from the discussion and the findings so recorded that both the Government pleader and the learned Subordinate Judge were suffering from total misconception and failed to appreciate the point at issue in suit. For example, it was argued that since all the recipients under the kabalas from Banalata Roy did not join as plaintiffs, the said fact proved that the kabalas in question did not create any title in favour of the plaintiffs and it is surprising that this atrocious submission found favour with the Subordinate Judge. I, therefore, find it unprofitable to refer to the exercise made by the learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment. 

 5. The learned Munsif seems to have written a least a better judgment. He did not believe the case as to the plaintiffs' title because the will under which the plaintiffs' vendor claimed title was not produced in the suit. It was noticed that in the probate proceeding also a draft will was filed the original was lost and the learned District Judge granted probate thereto. The learned Munsif held that the granting of the probate of the lost will was not conclusive proof of evidence of the will which was a vital document in this case. The learned Munsif further held that the plaintiff ought to have sought relief for establishment of their legal character and proved the same by the cogent evidence and that they failed to prove that their predecessor Banalata had acquired valid title to the suit land by the alleged will and by the granting of the probate on a lost will. It seems that the learned Munsif was under some misconception about the title of the plaintiffs' vendor, Banalata Roy. At the outsets it may be pointed out that the parties do not dispute that Niranjan Roy Barman was the owner of the suit property and Banalata Roy Barman was his wife. Now from the probate proceeding it is clear that a will executed by Niranjan Roy Barman in favour of Banalata Roy Barman was probated by the District Judge by order dated 3-4-72. Now, what is the effect of granting probate to the said will (a draft copy whereof was probated) by the District Judge? Admittedly, the proceedings In probate was not in issue in the suit. Section 41 of the Evidence act provides that a final judgment, order or decree of a competent Court, in the exercise of probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction, which confers upon or takes away from any person any legal character, or which declares any person to be entitled to any such character, or to be entitled to any specific thing, not a against any specified person but absolutely, is relevant when the existence of any such legal character, or the title of any such person to any such thing, is relevant. The section further provides that such judgment, order or decree is conclusive proof that any legal character which it confers accrued at the time when such judgment, order or decree came into operation. Section 91 of the said Act in Exception 2-provides that wills admitted to probate in Bangladesh may he proved by probate. The probate in the instant case was legally proved and could not be disputed which conclusively proved the legal character of the plaintiffs' vendor Banalata Roy as the executor of her husband's property. The production of the probate is, prima facie, evidence of title of the executor and the judgment in the probate 'proceeding is a judgment in rem. In this connection an observation of the judicial committee in the case of Soona Mayana Kena Roona Mayappa Chetty V. Nevena Supramanian Chetty, reported in A.I.R. 1916 (P.C.), 202 may be usefully referred to. The context was different but it was observed thus:- 

 In an old case of the Bombay High Court reported in ILR 1914 (Bombay), Vol-38, page 427 a Division Bench observed with respect of to the defendant's plea of forgery as to the will in question that "the title of the plaintiff was conclusively proved by the production of the probate, and it was no valid defence on the part of the first defendant to join in the allegation of the second defendant that the will was a forgery, and the probate had been obtained by fraud and deception". 

 6. From the above authorities it is clear that upon the production of the probate, the title of the plaintiffs' vendor was clearly established, she being the legal executor of her husband's property. It. was not at all necessary for the plaintiffs to pray for declaration of their title, not to speak of producing the will of Niranjan Roy Barman in this suit, so long as the probate granted by the District Judge remained valid. As a matter of fact, the defendant did not and could not question the genuineness of the will of Nirajan Roy Barman in favour of his wife Banalata Roy Barman in this suit. The judgment in the Probate proceeding being a judgment in rem will operate against the whole world. Thus, it must be said that the learned Munsif was not right in taking the view either that the will was required to be proved to establish Banalata's title or that the plffs. were required to establish their title in the suit. The plaintiffs' kabalas not being disputed, they have prima facie title to the suit land. 

 7. Both the courts below fell in error in taking the view that the plaintiffs' kabalas had no legal effect because the purchase was made after the order declaring the disputed property as enemy property was passed on 6-8-68 and there was a prohibition under the law for effecting transfer of an enemy property. Needless to say, the courts below were only begging flag question and the question was whether the property was an enemy property at all? Since there was a will in respect of the property in 1963 which was probated in probate case no. 270 of 1969 and Banalata Roy became the executor thereunder and it being nobody's case what Banalata Roy was an Indian national, there was no escape from the conclusion that the suit property at no point of time became enemy property. That being so all the laws, relating to enemy property and all the orders passed by the defendants upon the assumption, that the disputed property was enemy property were of no avail. The learned Munsif in his judgment referred to one decision reported in 21 D.L.R. 331 which upon scrutiny is found to-be wholly inapplicable in the facts of the present case. As to the question of limitation, the, learned Munsif was obviously wrong for the simple reason that the order dated 6-8-68 of the defendant No.2 was not required to be set aside since it was a void order and, indeed, the plaintiffs only asked for a declaration in respect of the said order and never prayed for setting aside of the same. Therefore, Article 14 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application as was wrongly held by the learned Munsif. Plaintiffs' possession was threatened by memo dated 29-8-73 of the defendant no.1 and on the following day they filed the suit, inter-alia for permanent injunction. Thus, there was no question of limitation. In view of the discussion above. I hold that the courts below committed palpable errors of law in deciding the suit which have affected the decision on merit. It is found that the suit is maintainable and not barred by limitation. The plaintiffs have amply proved their case and are entitled to the decree prayed for. 

 9. Let the defendants be restrained by an order of injunction from interfering with the plaintiff’s peaceful possession in the suit property and giving effect to Memo. No. 635(3) dated 29-8-73.
